deep.reconstruction:
Context: a 1953 manuscript on rearrangement-invariant convex functionals, called here 'fonctions de Pólya' and 'fonctions de Weyl', on spaces such as L^∞(]0,ω[). The previous page proves a representation theorem. A Pólya/Weyl functional P, meaning a convex, lower-semicontinuous, rearrangement-invariant functional that is increasing, can be written P(f) = sup_i (a_i + ∫_0^ω φ_i φ_f). Here φ_f is the decreasing rearrangement of |f| and the φ_i are positive decreasing L^1 functions.

Top of this page: it ends an example. For W(f) = ∫|f|^p, the condition W(f) < ∞ is equivalent to N_p(f) < ∞, i.e. f ∈ L^p.

§3, 'Inégalités linéaires sur fonctions de Weyl', states Prop. 4. Let ω < ∞ and let f, g be positive, decreasing, bounded functions on ]0,ω[. Suppose ∫_0^t f ≤ ∫_0^t g for 0 ≤ t ≤ ω, which is weak majorization f ≺_w g. Then P(f) ≤ P(g) for every increasing Weyl function P on L^∞(]0,ω[).

The converse is trivial: for each fixed t, f ↦ ∫_0^t φ_f (the Ky Fan-type functional) is itself an increasing Weyl function.

Proof. By the representation (1) of the previous page, and since φ_f = f for decreasing positive f, it suffices to show ∫ fφ ≤ ∫ gφ for every positive decreasing φ. This follows by integration by parts (continuous Abel summation). With F(t) = ∫_0^t f, one gets ∫_0^ω fφ = φ(ω)F(ω) + ∫_0^ω F d(−φ). Here −dφ is a positive measure and φ(ω) ≥ 0, so F ≤ G gives the inequality.

Remark ①: if F(ω) = G(ω), i.e. full majorization f ≺ g, positivity of φ is unnecessary. This is the classical distinction between majorization and weak majorization.

The next page applies this to compare W(f) ≤ W(g) for functions on a measure space M via their rearrangements. This is the material later published as Grothendieck's Bourbaki exposé on rearrangements and convexity inequalities in von Neumann algebras with trace.
errors: Minor gap: the boundary term at 0 in the integration by parts is not discussed. If φ is in L^1 but unbounded near 0, one needs F(t)φ(t) → 0. This holds because F(t) ≤ ||f||_∞ t and tφ(t) ≤ ∫_0^t φ → 0, so the argument is fine.
φ(ω) should be read as the left limit φ(ω−). This is harmless.

ideas.what: Weak majorization ∫_0^t f* ≤ ∫_0^t g* implies P(f) ≤ P(g) for every increasing convex rearrangement-invariant functional P, with converse via the functionals ∫_0^t f*.
ideas.modern_name: Continuous Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya / Karamata / Weyl (weak) majorization theorem; Calderón–Ryff–Lorentz–Shimogaki order on decreasing rearrangements
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya (1929/1934), Karamata (1932), Weyl (1949), Ky Fan (1951); continuous/function-space versions by G. G. Lorentz, Luxemburg, Ryff (1960s), Calderón (1966)
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck, 'Réarrangements de fonctions et inégalités de convexité dans les algèbres de von Neumann munies d'une trace', Séminaire Bourbaki exposé 113 (1955)

ideas.what: Reduction to linear inequalities ∫fφ ≤ ∫gφ for decreasing positive φ via a sup-of-linear representation, proved by Abel/integration by parts; remark that the positivity of φ can be dropped when total integrals are equal.
ideas.modern_name: Abel summation proof of majorization; majorization vs weak majorization

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard majorization theorem with a textbook integration-by-parts proof. It is a draft of material Grothendieck published in his 1955 Bourbaki exposé on rearrangements and trace inequalities, so nothing here appears missing from the record.
transcription_corrections: Section title: 'fonctions de Weyl' was crossed out and rewritten above. The final title is 'Inégalités linéaires sur fonctions de Weyl.'

Prop 4 inserted words: 'soit ω<+∞' above 'Soient', and 'positives' above 'f, g' (written 'deux positives' before 'fonctions'). The parenthesis '(intégrables bornées)' appears as 'intégrables bornées' in the image.
Under the integral in (1) the word 'croissante' is written, attached to 'fonction de Weyl' as an increasing Weyl function.
'Or cet résultat provient de (1)' is more likely 'Or ce résultat provient de (1)'.
The machine transcription's 'En vertu de [?] (1)' likely refers to the formula (1) of the previous page (the representation), i.e. 'En vertu de Prop. 3, (1)'.
